title: How to Replace Music That Is Copyrighted Before an Ad Launch

body_markdown:
Replacing music that is copyrighted before an ad launch is not just an editing task. The replacement needs permission for the actual campaign, the original audio must disappear from every deliverable and the media team must publish the approved versions. A clean export does not help if yesterday’s draft is still scheduled to run.


The goal is not necessarily to find music without copyright. Most professional production music is protected. The goal is to use a composition and recording whose permissions cover your advertiser, placements, territories and campaign dates.


For business affairs, creative and paid media teams, the safest approach is a coordinated replacement workflow. Start by deciding whether the existing track truly needs to go, then work through licensing, editing, platform delivery and release approval without treating any one step as a substitute for the others.


## When to replace music that is copyrighted


Copyright protection alone does not make a track unusable. Replacement becomes necessary when the required permissions are missing, cannot be verified or cannot be expanded before launch.


The[U.S. Copyright Office’s guidance for musicians](https://www.copyright.gov/engage/musicians/) distinguishes two separate works: the musical composition and the sound recording. For an ad using an existing recording, clearance generally involves synchronization permission for the composition and master-use permission for that recording. One agreement may cover both, but only if the licensor has the necessary authority.


Check the existing paperwork before discarding an approved creative direction. A campaign-specific amendment might address a missing territory or paid-social placement. Conversely, purchasing a download, paying for streaming access or receiving an artist’s informal approval does not necessarily clear all relevant rights.


When assessing music that is copyrighted, treat an unresolved ownership share or an undocumented advertising permission as a launch blocker, not an editing detail. If the campaign can wait for clearance, keep that option open. If it cannot, begin the replacement process.


## 1. Freeze the affected versions and assign owners


Stop the affected ads from progressing while the replacement is underway. Pause scheduled publication, tell agencies and creator partners not to boost the original versions and identify who controls each advertising account.


Create a small asset register rather than relying on filenames in a shared folder. Record the creative ID, aspect ratio, language, duration, current music version, publishing destination and approval status. Include cutdowns, localized edits, influencer deliverables and alternate hooks.


Assign clear responsibilities:


-


**Business affairs or counsel:** Approves the license scope and any unresolved rights questions.


-


**Creative or post-production:** Replaces the audio and delivers version-controlled exports.


-


**Media operations:** Swaps assets, checks scheduled placements and confirms which versions will run.


-


**Campaign owner:** Authorizes launch after the required approvals are complete.


Keep an internal reference copy of the original and its approval history, with access restricted as appropriate. Do not erase records simply because the soundtrack is changing.


An inventory matters because replacing music that is copyrighted in the hero video does not remove it from a six-second cutdown, a creator’s existing post or an agency’s scheduled ad. The register becomes the handoff document for the entire fix.


## 2. Write the advertising brief before choosing another track


Give the replacement supplier a usage brief before anyone falls in love with another song. “Commercial use allowed” is not a complete description of a campaign.


The brief should identify the advertiser and product, where the ads will appear, who will publish them and how long the campaign will run. Include boosting from creator accounts, partner-account advertising and off-platform distribution where relevant.


Use the following checks to turn that brief into a licensing decision:


License dimension


What to confirm


Covered parties


The advertiser, agency, production company and relevant partners are permitted users


Media and placements


Paid social, online video, connected TV or other planned placements are covered


Creator distribution


Boosting and ads run through creator or partner accounts are authorized where needed


Territory


Permission covers the campaign’s distribution, not merely the editor’s location


Term


Start dates, end dates and any post-campaign availability are addressed


Versions and edits


Cutdowns, loops, localized versions and other planned adaptations are permitted


Limits and exclusions


Spend caps, impression limits, restricted industries and prohibited associations are acceptable


Administration


Attribution, channel registration and claim-resolution requirements can be satisfied


A replacement can still be music that is copyrighted and be suitable for the campaign. What matters is whether the written grant covers these uses and whether the supplier controls the rights it promises.


## 3. Choose a replacement route with verifiable rights


A production-music library, a commissioned track and a directly licensed recording can each work. Choose based on the rights available and the time needed to verify them, not just the purchase price.


**Production music:** Check the specific license tier. A subscription may distinguish personal projects, client work, paid advertising and larger distribution. Confirm whether an active subscription is required when licensing, publishing or both.


**Commissioned music:** Put ownership or license terms in writing. Address performers, samples, third-party material, revisions and the right to synchronize the finished recording with the campaign. Paying a composer does not by itself answer every ownership question.


**Public-domain material:** Verify the composition and recording separately. A public-domain composition can have a newly protected recording or arrangement, and status may differ across countries.


“Royalty-free” describes a licensing model, not the absence of copyright. Likewise, a track labeled “copyright-free” needs supporting terms. Creative Commons licenses vary: a noncommercial restriction is incompatible with an ordinary ad campaign, while other conditions require separate review.


When choosing music that is copyrighted, a clear advertising license is more useful than a reassuring label on a download page. The same distinction explains why[legally downloading a music file does not necessarily grant commercial permission](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/when-legal-music-downloads-still-require-commercial-permission) .


## 4. Verify the exact track and preserve the license record


Confirm the track title, composer or artist, recording version, supplier and relevant identifiers where available. An instrumental, remix and original recording may have different clearance requirements. A familiar melody played by a different performer still raises composition-rights questions.


If ownership is unclear, use a structured[search for the song’s composition and recording rights holders](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/copyright-search-how-to-find-who-owns-a-song-or-video) rather than treating an audio-recognition result as proof of ownership.


Save the executed agreement or applicable license terms, order confirmation, invoice, track identifier and correspondence resolving any scope questions. For online purchases, retain the license version applicable to the transaction. A receipt showing that money changed hands is not always enough to establish what use was authorized.


Automated copyright checkers cannot complete this review. A match can identify a potential rights issue, but no match does not establish permission. YouTube also explains that its upload checks are not final, since later claims or other issues can still arise.


Approve music that is copyrighted on the strength of the rights documentation, not a successful upload test. If supplier terms exclude the intended ad use, choose another license or another track before post-production locks the edit.


## 5. Re-edit the soundtrack without carrying over the original


Return to the project timeline and remove the original music from every relevant layer. Muting one visible track is insufficient if the song is also embedded in a nested sequence, a flattened video or a combined dialogue-and-music file.


Check branded intros, end cards, transitions, alternate sequences and imported creator footage. Listen to the full export, including the opening and closing frames, rather than reviewing only the section where the replacement is most obvious.


Where dialogue and music are mixed together, request clean dialogue stems or re-record the voiceover. Audio-separation tools can assist an edit, but residual original music means the replacement is incomplete. Pitch-shifting, slowing a song down or using a shorter excerpt does not itself supply permission.


Match the new track to the ad’s pacing, then review transitions, voiceover intelligibility and delivery specifications. Update captions or on-screen text if they reference the original lyrics or artist.


Replacing music that is copyrighted should produce a genuinely new approved soundtrack, not an altered version of the same uncleared recording. Give the final export a unique version identifier and connect it to the license record in the asset register.


## 6. Replace the assets inside each publishing workflow


Do not stop at delivering the new files. Media operations must confirm which assets each platform, agency and creator will actually publish.


Depending on the placement, changing audio may require a new upload, a new post or a new ad creative. Some placements inherit audio from an existing organic post. Others have separate uploaded media or platform-added sound that needs its own review.


A sound available to an individual creator is not automatically cleared for a brand’s paid campaign. Check the current platform terms and the intended account and placement. This is particularly relevant when[an organic creator post becomes a commercial music use through boosting or advertising](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/ugc-music-licensing-when-a-viral-sound-becomes-commercial) .


Update the asset register with the replacement file and the corresponding platform creative or post ID. Remove the old asset from active schedules, draft campaigns and reusable templates where it could be selected accidentally. Coordinate any claim-related channel registration required by the replacement licensor.


For campaigns replacing music that is copyrighted, the final platform asset is the release candidate. Review that version, not only the local master file. Leave room for platform processing and ad review; a soundtrack change can affect the launch timetable even when the license is settled.


## 7. Run a documented launch gate


Release approval should connect the licensed track, the edited file and the platform asset. A legal approval for one recording cannot validate an export containing another, and creative approval does not establish advertising rights.


Use a short preflight checklist:


-


**Rights confirmed:** The required composition and recording permissions cover the actual campaign.


-


**Evidence retained:** The applicable license, transaction record and relevant correspondence are saved.


-


**Audio verified:** The complete export has been checked for original music and unintended platform-added sound.


-


**Versions reconciled:** Every active placement points to an approved replacement asset.


-


**Term controls assigned:** Someone owns expiration tracking, renewals and any required removal or cessation of paid use.


-


**Approvals recorded:** Business affairs, creative and media operations have signed off within their responsibilities.


Document exceptions explicitly. If a territory remains uncleared, exclude it operationally and verify the exclusion rather than leaving a note that no one implements.


The release record for music that is copyrighted should make a straightforward question answerable: which permission supports the audio in this particular ad? If the team cannot connect those records, the campaign is not ready for release.


## If clearance will miss the launch deadline


Prepare an alternate creative that does not depend on the disputed music. Options include a voiceover-led edit with cleared sound effects, a newly approved production track or a silent treatment designed to work without a soundtrack. Each option still needs normal rights and quality review.


Do not replace a popular song with a deliberately close imitation and assume the issue is solved. Re-recording avoids use of the original master, but it does not automatically resolve rights in the composition.


If earlier versions have already run, preserve the relevant records and have counsel assess that use separately. Replacing the audio prospectively does not retroactively authorize earlier distribution.


Under deadline pressure, replacing music that is copyrighted is often easier when the team accepts a different creative direction. A simpler, properly cleared ad is a better launch candidate than a nearly identical edit with unresolved permissions.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does an ad need permission if it uses only a few seconds of a song?** There is no universal number of seconds that makes advertising use safe. Duration alone does not establish permission or fair use. Clear the intended use or select a replacement with suitable rights.


**Can I use royalty-free music in paid ads?** Often, but only if the particular license permits it. Check paid placements, client use, territory, duration and any limits on spend, impressions or distribution. Royalty-free does not mean unrestricted.


**Does recording a cover solve the problem?** A new recording may avoid using someone else’s master, but the composition remains a separate rights question. Do not assume a cover-song distribution license authorizes synchronization with an advertisement.


**Can a copyright checker approve the replacement?** No. For music that is copyrighted, automated checks can help identify matches or potential claims, but they cannot confirm your complete license scope or the supplier’s authority. Keep the written rights review separate from technical checks.


## Make the replacement traceable before you launch


Before releasing the campaign, connect three records: the music permission, the approved export and the live or scheduled platform asset. If one is missing, hold that placement until the gap is resolved. This gives the team a repeatable approval process rather than another last-minute soundtrack swap.
